title: No more of talk ... I now must change Those Notes to Tragic
short: The final invocation announces the end of friendly converse between God, angels and man, and a turn from epic narrative to tragedy.
body: 'No more of talk where God or Angel Guest With Man, as with his Friend, familiar us'd To sit indulgent'; the narrator 'now must change Those Notes to Tragic'. Verity notes that the next heavenly messenger will not be the 'affable' Raphael but the stern Michael, and that 'as with his friend' recalls God speaking to Moses 'as a man speaketh unto his friend' (Exodus 33:11). The word 'Tragic' is pointed: Milton had first planned the Fall as a tragedy, and drafts of 'Adam Unparadiz'd' survive in the Trinity College manuscript; he later prefaced Samson Agonistes with an essay on tragedy, which the Dartmouth edition cites alongside Aristotle's Poetics. The 'Tragic' notes are 'foul distrust, and breach Disloyal' on man's part, and on Heaven's 'Anger and just rebuke', bringing 'Sin and her shadow Death' into the world.

title: argument Not less but more Heroic then the wrath Of stern Achilles
short: Milton claims his subject is more heroic than the wrath of Achilles, the rage of Turnus, or the anger of Neptune and Juno that drives Odysseus and Aeneas.
body: The Fall is an 'argument Not less but more Heroic then the wrath Of stern Achilles on his Foe pursu'd Thrice Fugitive about Troy Wall; or rage Of Turnus for Lavinia disespous'd, Or Neptun's ire or Juno's, that so long Perplex'd the Greek and Cytherea's Son'. Verity identifies each epic: the Iliad, which begins with Achilles' wrath and narrates his pursuit of Hector three times round Troy (Book 22); the Aeneid's Turnus, whose promised bride Lavinia was given to Aeneas; the Odyssey, where Neptune's anger delays Odysseus ('the Greek'); and the Aeneid's Juno, who persecutes Aeneas, son of Cytherea (Venus). Each classical subject is an anger. Milton's subject is also about wrath, God's 'Anger and just rebuke', but it concerns the whole human race, and its true heroism lies elsewhere (9.31-33).

title: my Celestial Patroness ... Easie my unpremeditated Verse
short: The poet's Muse visits him 'nightly' and dictates his verse 'unpremeditated' as he sleeps, an account matching reports of Milton's methods of composition.
body: The heavenly Muse, his 'Celestial Patroness', 'deignes Her nightly visitation unimplor'd, And dictates to me slumbring, or inspires Easie my unpremeditated Verse'. Verity identifies the patroness with Urania (1.6; 7.1) and cross-refers to the poet's claims to be inspired at night or at dawn (3.29-32; 7.28-30). Early biographers, cited by Verity in his notes on Book III, reported that the blind Milton composed lines in the night and dictated them in the morning to whoever was at hand. Verity quotes Newton's defence of these personal passages, which some critics thought out of place in epic: 'when I admire the author I desire to know something of the man'. The inverted stress on 'Easie', Verity notes, makes the rhythm itself easy.

title: Warrs ... with long and tedious havoc fabl'd Knights
short: Milton rejects the traditional epic matter of battles and chivalric romance in favour of 'the better fortitude Of Patience and Heroic Martyrdom'.
body: Milton says he is 'Not sedulous by Nature to indite Warrs, hitherto the onely Argument Heroic deem'd', whose chief art was 'to dissect With long and tedious havoc fabl'd Knights In Battels feign'd', while 'the better fortitude Of Patience and Heroic Martyrdom Unsung' remains. He also dismisses 'Races and Games, Or tilting Furniture, emblazon'd Shields, Impreses quaint, Caparisons and Steeds', the matter of Boiardo, Ariosto, Tasso and Spenser (Verity), along with Homeric and Virgilian games. Verity suggests that the 'fabled' character of the Arthurian legend helped turn Milton from his early plan of an Arthurian epic. The Dartmouth edition notes the redefinition of heroism as spiritual resistance to temptation, exemplified by Abdiel and finally by the Son. Ironically, the poem itself contains a war in Heaven and infernal games.

title: an age too late, or cold Climat, or Years
short: The poet fears that the world's decline, England's cold climate or his own age may weaken his 'intended wing'.
body: Unless the Muse supports him, the poet fears that 'an age too late, or cold Climat, or Years damp my intended wing Deprest'. Verity explains each: a widespread seventeenth-century belief, mocked by Johnson, that nature and mankind were decaying (Godfrey Goodman's The Fall of Man, 1616, argued it); Milton's lifelong opinion that northern climates hindered genius, voiced in Mansus, The Reason of Church Government and his History of Britain, which the Dartmouth edition traces to Aristotle's claim that northern peoples lack intelligence (Politics 7.7, 1327b); and his own age, since he was nearing sixty. 'Deprest' answers 'raise' in the line before: the flight imagery of the invocations returns for the last time.

title: Satan's seven nights: Pontus, Maeotis, the River Ob, Orontes, Darien, Ganges and Indus
short: To avoid detection Satan circles the globe in darkness for seven nights, from the Black Sea and Siberia to Panama and India.
body: Satan spends 'seven continu'd Nights' riding with the darkness: three circling the equator and four running along the colures, the great circles through the poles, as Masson explained (quoted by Verity). Geographically, he goes north 'over Pontus' (the Black Sea) and 'the Poole Maeotis' (the Sea of Azov, Latin Palus Maeotis, 'pool'), 'beyond the River Ob' in Siberia, which Milton also mentions in his History of Moscovia, then south to the Antarctic; and from west to east from the Syrian Orontes to 'Darien' (the isthmus of Panama), and so round to 'Ganges and Indus'. Verity notes Masson's point that the Ganges would be reached before the Indus on that circuit. The catalogue shows Satan's restless, circling motion and Milton's interest in contemporary geography.

anchor: The Serpent suttlest Beast of all the Field
title: The Serpent suttlest Beast of all the Field
short: Satan chooses the serpent as his disguise because it is 'subtil' (Genesis 3:1), so that its cleverness will not arouse suspicion.
body: Satan 'consider'd every Creature, which of all Most opportune might serve his Wiles, and found The Serpent suttlest Beast of all the Field'. The phrase is Genesis 3:1, 'Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the Lord God had made', as Verity and the Dartmouth edition note. Milton's interpretation answers an old question: why a serpent? Because 'in the wilie Snake, Whatever sleights none would suspicious mark, As from his wit and native suttletie Proceeding' (9.91-93). The unfallen serpent is not evil, and in Eden it is beautiful, moving upright 'on his reare, Circular base of rising foulds' (9.497-98). Satan's entry into it, 'incarnate and imbrute', is for him a degradation he resents (9.163-71), a dark parody of the Son's incarnation.

title: Let us divide our labours: the separation scene
short: Eve proposes that they work apart; Adam objects but finally lets her go. The debate tests the meaning of free, untested virtue.
body: Eve suggests they divide the gardening so as to get more done; Adam fears the enemy will find her alone. Eve, hurt, argues that a virtue never tested is no virtue: 'And what is Faith, Love, Vertue unassaid Alone, without exterior help sustaind?' (9.335-36). Verity and the Dartmouth edition note how close this is to Milton's own Areopagitica: 'I cannot praise a fugitive and cloister'd vertue, unexercis'd and unbreath'd'. Adam replies that 'God left free the Will' but that reason may be deceived, and finally consents: 'Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more' (9.372). Critics are divided over who is right: whether Adam fails in his duty to command, or rightly respects Eve's freedom; and whether Eve's argument is sound principle wrongly applied.

title: Delia's self ... Pales, or Pomona ... Ceres in her Prime
greek: Latin Pales, Pomona, Ceres; Delia (Artemis of Delos)
short: Leaving Adam, Eve is compared to a wood-nymph, to Diana, and, armed with garden tools, to the Roman goddesses of flocks, fruit and grain.
body: As Eve withdraws she is like an 'Oread or Dryad, or of Delia's Traine', but surpasses Delia (Diana, born on Delos) herself in 'Goddess-like deport'. With her garden tools she is likest 'To Pales, or Pomona', Roman goddesses of flocks and fruit, 'Pomona when she fled Vertumnus', or 'Ceres in her Prime, Yet Virgin of Proserpina from Jove'. Verity explains each: Pales the goddess of shepherds; Pomona, wooed and finally won by the shape-changing Vertumnus (Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.623-771); Ceres before she bore Proserpina. Verity quotes Pearce's observation that the first comparisons fit Eve's gait, the later ones her tools. But each figure also hints at pursuit, seduction or rape, preparing for the disguised tempter: Vertumnus, like Satan, wins his goddess through a disguise.

anchor: Her self, though fairest unsupported Flour
title: Her self, though fairest unsupported Flour
short: Satan finds Eve propping up her drooping flowers, herself an unsupported flower: the line echoes Proserpina 'her self a fairer Floure' in Book IV.
body: Satan finds Eve alone among her roses, 'oft stooping to support Each Flour of slender stalk', 'mindless the while, Her self, though fairest unsupported Flour, From her best prop so farr, and storm so nigh'. Verity notes that the line repeats the image of 4.270, where Proserpina gathering flowers was 'her self a fairer Floure' before 'gloomie Dis' carried her off. The metaphor joins Eve to her work (she tends what she resembles) and marks her vulnerability: Adam, her 'best prop', is far away. 'Mindless' means unaware. The gentle irony that she supports others while unsupported herself gives the scene its pathos and keeps the narrator's sympathy with Eve even as he foreshadows the danger.

title: Gardens feign'd Or of reviv'd Adonis, or renownd Alcinous ... the Sapient King
short: Eve's flower-garden surpasses the mythical gardens of Adonis and Alcinous and the scriptural garden where Solomon courted his Egyptian bride.
body: The spot is 'delicious' beyond 'those Gardens feign'd Or of reviv'd Adonis, or renownd Alcinous, host of old Laertes Son, Or that, not Mystic, where the Sapient King Held dalliance with his fair Egyptian Spouse'. The gardens of Adonis were proverbial (Spenser describes one in Faerie Queene 3.6); Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, entertained Odysseus, son of Laertes, in his orchard of perpetual fruit (Odyssey 7.112-32), as Verity notes. The 'Sapient King' is Solomon, whose garden appears in the Song of Solomon (6:2) and whose Egyptian wife was Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kings 3:1); Verity explains that 'not Mystic' distinguishes this real, scriptural garden from the 'feign'd' classical ones. The Dartmouth edition notes the comparison. 'Dalliance' here is innocent, but Solomon's foreign wives led him to idolatry (1.444-46).

anchor: As one who long in populous City pent
title: As one who long in populous City pent
short: Satan's delight at the garden and at Eve is compared to a city-dweller breathing country air on a summer morning, perhaps drawn from Milton's London youth.
body: Satan feels like 'one who long in populous City pent, Where Houses thick and Sewers annoy the Aire', who goes out on a summer morning among the villages and farms, where 'each rural sight, each rural sound' delights him, and above all a passing 'fair Virgin'. Verity cites Keightley's suggestion that this may record Milton's own experience as a young man living in Bread Street in the City of London, and Milton's seventh Latin elegy on walks in the suburbs; 'annoy' means pollute and 'tedded' means spread to dry. The simile is unusual because it gives Satan a moment of ordinary human pleasure, which the narrator then follows with his momentary disarming.

title: Stupidly good, of enmitie disarm'd
short: For a moment Eve's beauty and innocence leave Satan 'stupidly good', stunned out of his malice, before hate returns.
body: Eve's 'graceful Innocence' overawes 'His Malice', so that 'the Evil one abstracted stood From his own evil, and for the time remaind Stupidly good, of enmitie disarm'd, Of guile, of hate, of envie, of revenge'. 'Stupidly' keeps its Latin sense of stupor, a state of being struck senseless with amazement, not mere foolishness. The Dartmouth edition compares the power of chastity in Comus (450-52) and Tarquin's hesitation before the sleeping Lucrece in Shakespeare's poem. The moment is brief: 'the hot Hell that alwayes in him burnes' returns and he recalls his purpose. Like the soliloquy on Niphates, the episode shows Satan capable of goodness yet choosing evil, which makes his choice more culpable and more tragic.

title: Hermione and Cadmus ... the God In Epidaurus ... Ammonian Jove, or Capitoline
short: The serpent is lovelier than every famous serpent of myth: Cadmus and his wife transformed, Aesculapius at Epidaurus, and the snake-gods said to have fathered Alexander and Scipio.
body: Verity, quoting Keightley, lists the serpents of antiquity: Cadmus, founder of Thebes, and his wife Harmonia ('Hermione') changed into serpents in Illyria (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.563-603); Aesculapius, god of healing, who came from Epidaurus to Rome in serpent form to end a plague (Metamorphoses 15.622-744); and the serpent-gods who, in legend, fathered great men: Jupiter Ammon, said by Plutarch to have visited Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, and Jupiter Capitolinus, said to have fathered Scipio Africanus, 'the highth of Rome'. The list places Satan's disguise among stories of divine seduction and metamorphosis, and Verity notes that Milton recalled the Cadmus episode again for the devils' transformation in Book X.

title: the Herd disguis'd ... at Circean call
short: The animals obey Eve more meekly than Circe's beasts, men she had transformed by magic: an image of enchantment and servitude.
body: The serpent approaches; Eve does not notice, used to the animals 'that at her call, More duteous ... then at Circean call the Herd disguis'd'. Circe, the enchantress of the Odyssey, changed Odysseus' men into swine with drugs and her wand (Odyssey 10.210-43), so that her herd was really men 'disguis'd'. Verity explains the allusion and notes that Milton had made Comus Circe's son and used 'the Circean cup of servitude' in Eikonoklastes for the nation's infatuation with monarchy. The comparison reverses roles: Eve's mastery of the animals is innocent, but the creature now approaching is the real enchanter, and the scene is about to turn her into the one charmed.

title: As when of old som Orator renound ... O Sacred, Wise, and Wisdom-giving Plant, Mother of Science
short: Satan addresses the tree like a classical orator of Athens or 'free Rome', worshipping it as 'Mother of Science': the climax of the temptation.
body: Satan composes himself 'As when of old som Orator renound In Athens or free Rome, where Eloquence Flourishd', and begins 'in highth', plunging into his subject without preamble. Verity suggests Demosthenes, Isocrates and Cicero, whose first Catilinarian begins abruptly ('Quousque tandem...'); the Dartmouth edition notes that Milton admired the orators of the free republics and that Satan abuses their art. He hails the tree: 'O Sacred, Wise, and Wisdom-giving Plant, Mother of Science'. 'Science' means knowledge in general (Latin scientia), and Verity hears Virgil's 'happy he who could know the causes of things' (Georgics 2.490). The arguments that follow (the serpent has eaten and lives; God would not punish so petty a trespass; God forbids only out of envy) form a sophistical masterpiece.

title: Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat Sighing
short: As Eve eats, Earth feels the wound and Nature sighs; when Adam eats, Earth trembles again: the classical portent made cosmic.
body: 'So saying, her rash hand in evil hour Forth reaching to the Fruit, she pluck'd, she eat: Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat Sighing through all her Works gave signs of woe, That all was lost'. Verity notes the pathetic alliteration and explains that Milton imitates the portents of classical epic at the turning points of his poem: compare the earth's trembling when Adam eats (9.1000-04) and the omens of 11.182-207. He quotes Addison: these are not mere prodigies but 'marks of her sympathising in the fall of man'. A model may be Virgil's description of the union of Dido and Aeneas, when Earth and Juno gave the signal and lightning flashed (Aeneid 4.166-68). Verity also notes that the only use of 'Original' sin in the poem comes at 9.1003-04.

title: the plant sciential sap, deriv'd From Nectar, drink of Gods
short: Eve bows to the tree as if its sap held divine knowledge: her first act after the Fall is idolatry.
body: Having eaten, Eve plans to tend the tree each morning and bows to it 'as to the power That dwelt within, whose presence had infus'd Into the plant sciential sap, deriv'd From Nectar, drink of Gods'. 'Sciential' means knowledge-giving (Verity; Dartmouth). Verity notes Charles Lamb's playful memory of 'those sciential apples' in his essay Oxford in the Vacation. The worship of the tree fulfils Raphael's warnings about temperance in knowledge (7.126-30) and enacts the catalogue of Book I in miniature: the first fallen act of humankind is to treat a created thing as divine. Eve also considers keeping the knowledge to herself to become 'more equal' to Adam, then decides he must share her fate, lest he wed 'another Eve' (9.817-33), a passage Verity uses to discuss Milton's view of the sexes.

title: From his slack hand the Garland wreath'd for Eve Down drop'd, and all the faded Roses shed
short: Adam drops the garland he made for Eve when he sees what she has done; its roses fade, an image of the loss of Paradise.
body: While Eve is away, Adam weaves 'Of choicest Flours a Garland to adorne Her Tresses' (9.840-41). When he meets her and hears her story, 'Astonied stood and Blank', and 'From his slack hand the Garland wreath'd for Eve Down drop'd, and all the faded Roses shed'. Verity notes that 'astonied' is the old form of 'astonished' (Job 17:8) and that the strong pause at 9.888 marks Adam's horror. The garland belongs to wedding imagery (Eve was earlier 'more lovely then Pandora' in her bower); its withering is the visible first death in the poem. The narrator's speed, 'all the faded Roses shed', contrasts with the unfading amaranth of Heaven (3.353-57), and anticipates the death that Eve, 'Defac't, deflourd, and now to Death devote' (9.901), has brought on herself.

anchor: The Link of Nature draw me
title: I feel The Link of Nature draw me: Flesh of Flesh, Bone of my Bone thou art
short: Adam resolves at once to die with Eve, repeating his wedding words of Book VIII: their bond of nature outweighs his obedience to God.
body: Adam's inward speech decides in a moment: 'with thee Certain my resolution is to Die; How can I live without thee?' 'I feel The Link of Nature draw me: Flesh of Flesh, Bone of my Bone thou art, and from thy State Mine never shall be parted, bliss or woe'. Verity refers back to Adam's greeting at 8.494-96 ('Bone of my Bone'); the Dartmouth edition hears the marriage vow 'for better, for worse'. The reasoning is moving and generous, but it reverses the priorities Raphael urged: love for Eve has displaced love for God. Eve praises this 'glorious trial of exceeding Love' (9.961), and critics have long debated whether Adam's choice is noble self-sacrifice, uxorious idolatry, or both. He might have interceded for her, as the Son does for mankind in Book III.

title: he scrupl'd not to eat Against his better knowledge, not deceav'd, But fondly overcome with Femal charm
short: Adam eats knowingly, 'not deceav'd' (1 Timothy 2:14), but 'fondly' (foolishly) overcome by Eve's charm. Earth trembles a second time.
body: 'He scrupl'd not to eat Against his better knowledge, not deceav'd, But fondly overcome with Femal charm'. Verity cites 1 Timothy 2:14, 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression', and notes that Adam sinned wilfully; the Dartmouth edition also cites Augustine's City of God (14.11). 'Fondly' means foolishly as well as lovingly. Verity cross-refers to the Son's judgment, which takes up exactly this point (10.145-56). Nature responds: 'Earth trembl'd from her entrails, as again In pangs, and Nature gave a second groan, Skie lowr'd, and muttering Thunder, som sad drops Wept at compleating of the mortal Sin Original' (9.1000-04). The Dartmouth edition notes, without endorsing it as intentional, that this is line 999, the inversion of 666 at which Death is introduced in Book II.

title: So rose the Danite strong Herculean Samson from the Harlot-lap Of Philistean Dalilah
short: Waking from lustful sleep, Adam and Eve find their innocence gone, like Samson rising shorn of his strength from Delilah's lap.
body: After their first fallen lovemaking, 'in Lust they burne', the couple wake to shame: 'So rose the Danite strong Herculean Samson from the Harlot-lap Of Philistean Dalilah, and wak'd Shorn of his strength, They destitute and bare Of all thir vertue'. Samson, of the tribe of Dan (Judges 13:2), revealed the secret of his strength to Delilah, who had his hair shaved as he slept (Judges 16:4-20); Verity gives the references and notes Milton's earlier uses of the story and his scansion of 'Dalilah'. 'Herculean' compares Samson with Hercules, often treated as his classical counterpart. The Dartmouth edition observes that the plural 'They' makes both Adam and Eve Samson-like. Milton's own drama Samson Agonistes (1671) returned to the story.

title: The Fig-tree ... In Malabar or Decan ... Columbus found th' American so girt
short: Adam and Eve cover themselves with leaves of the Indian banyan fig, and are compared to the feather-girt natives Columbus found in America.
body: They choose 'The Figtree, not that kind for Fruit renown'd, But such as at this day to Indians known In Malabar or Decan spreds her Armes Branching so broad and long, that in the ground The bended Twigs take root'. This is the banyan, whose rooting branches were described by Pliny (Natural History 12.22) and by Renaissance herbalists; Verity glosses 'Decan' (the Deccan) as a name for the Indian peninsula. The leaves are 'broad as Amazonian Targe', the crescent shields of the Amazons (Aeneid 1.490). Genesis 3:7 says they 'sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons'. The comparison to 'th' American' whom 'Columbus found ... so girt With featherd Cincture' is pointed: as the Dartmouth edition notes, Milton resists the idea of the American peoples as unfallen innocents.
